name: Gareth Petrov

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for meeting me, Gareth. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government, and what you say stays confidential. You can tell me your public line and, separately, what you really think. What does a normal working day look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I manage the farm side of the Thornbury Estate: 900 acres, 250 Aberdeen Angus cattle, wheat and barley, and some woodland I keep an eye on. I'm up at half six, check the cattle, then sort the day with the three men on the team. On the side I run Petrov Beef Boxes, selling beef from the estate's cull cows straight to families, and I use AI every day for the orders, the emails and the adverts.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like building something. The beef boxes started with twelve customers and now it's two hundred, and the estate gets a cut, so everyone's happy. What wears me out is red tape, the forms for moving cattle and the rules for selling meat. I live with my girlfriend Chloe, who's a hairdresser in town, in a rented flat, and we've got about three months' savings because I keep putting money back into the boxes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say AI's a handy tool for a small business and that's all it needs to be. On the beef box page I'd post that we still raise cattle the old way. At the pub I'd say don't believe everything the tech companies say.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's good for me. The tools save me hours on the beef boxes, and the estate job is solid. My only pressure is that the savings are thin because I keep investing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd grow the beef boxes to 300 customers over the year, with AI writing the adverts and handling the orders. I'd buy a second chest freezer, about 900. And I'd put 100 a month aside so we get to four months' savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Busy and happy, really.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does Chloe think of the beef boxes?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Chloe says I talk about them more than I talk about her, which is fair. She does the photos, though, so she's in it as much as me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything you'd worry about in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The estate changing hands, maybe. The old Colonel is 80, and his nephew might want to sell the farmland. But I'd have the boxes, and good managers always find work.

say: AI is a **handy tool** for a small business, nothing more.
We still raise **cattle the old way**.
Don't believe everything the **tech companies** say.
think: The tools save me **hours** on the beef boxes.
My only pressure is **thin savings** from reinvesting.
The **estate job** feels solid in this picture.
do: **Grow** the beef boxes to **300 customers** this year.
**Buy** a second chest freezer for about **900**.
**Save** 100 a month to reach four months' cushion.
fieldNote: He uses AI to build a **side business**, which makes him feel in control.
He is **confident** in his own value as a manager.
His one worry is the **estate** changing hands.

steps.text: Grow Petrov Beef Boxes to 300 customers this year
Buy a second chest freezer for about 900
Put 100 a month aside towards four months' savings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the second one. This one's called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is a chance for small businesses to compete with the big boys. On the beef box page I'd post about how we use AI for the boring bits, so we can spend more time with the cattle. I'd tell other farmers to stop moaning and get on with it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it suits me. The thinking jobs, orders, booking the abattoir, the emails, I'd hand them all to AI. The estate job is mostly hands-on, so robots are a long way off, and I'd have time to grow the business.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd set the beef box business up to run almost on its own, with AI handling orders, delivery routes and customer questions. I'd invest in a small cold room, about 6,000, with a loan. And I'd pitch the estate on letting me sell beef from the whole herd, not just the culls.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Good. A bit of a thrill, honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Taking a 6,000 loan with three months' savings is a risk. What if it goes wrong?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd sell the cold room and pay it back. I've still got my wage from the estate, which is the whole point of keeping the day job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Bob, our oldest stockman. Bob's 61 and can't stand screens, and if the estate brings in tablets for everything, he'll struggle. I'd want him kept on for the cattle work he's brilliant at.

say: This is a **chance** for small businesses to compete.
Farmers should **stop moaning** and get on with it.
think: The **thinking jobs** for the beef boxes can all go to AI.
Robots for the **hands-on** estate work are a long way off.
do: **Set up** AI to run beef box orders and **delivery routes**.
**Borrow** about **6,000** for a small cold room.
**Pitch** the estate on selling beef from the **whole herd**.
S1.quote: I've still got my wage from the estate, which is the whole point of keeping the day job.
fieldNote: He sees Steady Disruption as an **opportunity**, not a threat.
He takes on **debt** with his estate wage as a safety net.
He looks out for **Bob**, the older stockman, showing his loyalty.

steps.text: Hand beef box orders and delivery routes to AI
Borrow about 6,000 to build a small cold room
Ask the estate to sell beef from the whole Angus herd

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one moves much faster. This one's called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say get moving, because waiting is the only real mistake. On the beef box page I'd say we're still real people with real cattle. I'd say government should keep out of the way and let businesses adapt.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, this one bothers me. If AI can run any small business by 2028, then anyone can run a beef box company, and the big firms will do it cheaper. By 2031 the estate could use robots for the cattle, and the Colonel's nephew would sell me off with the farm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop borrowing straight away and build our savings to six months. I'd lock in long contracts with my best customers and the local butcher, so the boxes have a base. And I'd try to rent 50 acres of my own, so I've got land and cattle if the estate job goes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I'd still feel like I'm steering, but there'd be a lot of rocks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said government should keep out of the way. Would you take help if it was offered?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For a business loan, yes, I'm not proud. But I wouldn't want a handout to sit at home. I'd want something that helps me build.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Chloe?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Chloe her hairdressing is safer than my job, which would make her laugh. A robot cutting hair in a small town is a long way off, I reckon.

say: Get moving, because **waiting** is the only real mistake.
We're still **real people** with real cattle.
think: By **2028** anyone could run a beef box business with AI.
By **2031** robots could replace me on the **estate**.
do: **Stop borrowing** and build savings to **six months**.
**Lock in** long contracts with top customers and the butcher.
**Rent** about **50 acres** of my own land.
feel: Anxious, still steering but with **a lot of rocks**.
S2.quote: If AI can run any small business by 2028, then anyone can run a beef box company, and the big firms will do it cheaper.
fieldNote: The short warning threatens both his **job** and his **side business**.
He reaches for **land** as something AI can't copy.
He'd take a **loan**, not a handout, true to his views.

steps.text: Stop borrowing and build savings to six months
Sign long contracts with top beef box customers and the butcher
Rent about 50 acres to run some cattle of his own

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now the slower version. This one's called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a head start for anyone with sense. On the page I'd say we're building a farm business that lasts. I'd tell the young lads to learn the robots as well as the cattle.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's manageable. The AI would take the business side by 2031, which levels the field, but I'd have five years to build a name customers trust. The estate robots come around 2034, and by then I'd want my own land.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd grow the beef boxes steadily and put the profit into renting land, about 50 acres within three years. I'd keep the estate job as long as it pays. I'd use AI for everything on the business side, as I do now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but more excited than worried.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why would a customer pick your boxes if anyone can set one up?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because they've met me at the farm open day and seen the cattle. People still want to buy beef from a man they can shake hands with.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you and Chloe change any plans?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd hold off on a wedding until the land is sorted, maybe two years. Chloe's fine with that, as long as I actually ask her.

say: Five years is a **head start** for anyone with sense.
Young workers should learn **robots and cattle** together.
think: AI **levels the field** for small businesses by **2031**.
I'd want **my own land** before estate robots in 2034.
do: **Grow** the beef boxes and put profit into **renting land**.
**Keep** the estate job as long as it pays.
**Delay** a wedding with Chloe until the land is sorted.
S3.quote: People still want to buy beef from a man they can shake hands with.
fieldNote: Five years lets him build a **trusted name** before AI levels the field.
**Land** is his long-term answer to robots.
He'd **delay** family plans for the business.

steps.text: Rent about 50 acres within three years
Grow Petrov Beef Boxes with profits reinvested
Put off the wedding with Chloe for about two years

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And the last one. This one's called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty, and anyone who isn't ready only has themselves to blame. On the page I'd say we're planning for the long run. I'd encourage other young farmers to start something of their own.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, this is a good one for me. By 2039 I'd want my own farm with cattle and robots, and the beef boxes as the shop window. I'd be 37 when AGI arrives, with years of business behind me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd grow the boxes, rent land in about five years, and buy a couple of farm robots when they're cheap enough. I'd marry Chloe in the next couple of years. I'd keep the estate job until my own place could pay me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Pretty fired up, actually.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything that worries you here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Land prices, if everyone decides land is the safe bet. And the Colonel's nephew, still. But ten years is long enough to work around both.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want people to understand about farmers like you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We're not scared of change, most of us. Farmers like me just want to own the change instead of having it done to us.

say: **Ten years** is plenty, so there's no excuse for not being ready.
Young farmers should start **something of their own**.
think: By **2039** I'd want my **own farm** with cattle and robots.
I'd be 37 when AGI arrives, with **years of business** behind me.
do: **Rent** my own land in about **five years**.
**Marry** Chloe in the next couple of years.
S4.quote: Farmers like me just want to own the change instead of having it done to us.
fieldNote: With ten years, he sees AGI as a **business opportunity**.
He still watches **land prices** and the estate's future.
He sees farmers as wanting **ownership** of change.

steps.text: Rent land of his own in about five years
Buy a couple of farm robots once prices fall
Marry Chloe within the next couple of years

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because my job and my side business would both be under pressure at once. What would help is cheaper land rents for young farmers and less red tape for selling meat direct, so small people can move fast.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the cattle themselves. An Angus cow lives fifteen years. Whatever we decide about robots, somebody has to plan for cattle that outlive the next three governments.

headlineQuote: Whatever we decide about robots, somebody has to plan for cattle that outlive the next three governments.
portrait: Gareth is a **27-year-old** manager of a 900-acre estate farm with 250 Angus cattle.
He runs a growing **beef box** side business and uses AI every day for it.
He lives with Chloe, a **hairdresser**, and keeps savings thin by reinvesting.
He is calm in most scenarios and **anxious** in AGI by 2028, when job and business are both hit.
He wants **his own land** and favours loans and freedom over handouts.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because his job and side business would be hit at once.
whatWouldHelp: Less **red tape** for selling meat direct.
